facts.text: The simulations independently varied Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr among 0, 10, 20, and 30 at.%, assigning the compositional balance to Hf, to produce 13 unique alloys.
Temperature-dependent mechanical and thermal-expansion tests were performed specifically on the optimized Nb10, Ta10, and Ti0 compositions.
Uniaxial tension was applied along the z direction at a strain rate of 1 × 10^8 s^-1, with the principal composition comparisons conducted at 300 K.
Temperature-dependent tests covered 300–1200 K in 300 K increments, and thermal-expansion simulations used a heating rate of 0.02 K/fs.
The authors attributed strengthening at low Nb or Ta content to substitutional solid-solution strengthening that impedes dislocation motion.
Elevated temperature increased lattice vibrations and facilitated dislocation migration, thereby reducing strength and stiffness.
Tensile failure involved bond breaking and shear localization near 45° to the loading direction, producing cup-and-cone-type ductile fracture.
Reducing Nb or Ta from 20 to 10 at.% increased ultimate tensile strength and elastic modulus relative to the equimolar alloy, whereas increasing either element to 30 at.% reduced both properties.
At 300 K, Nb10 had a UTS of 3.8 GPa and an elastic modulus of 137.7 ± 3 GPa, compared with 2.9 GPa and 117.7 ± 3 GPa for the equimolar baseline.
At 300 K, Ta10 reached a UTS of 3.9 GPa, a modulus of 129.1 ± 3 GPa, and an elongation of 25.51%, versus 17.0% elongation for the equimolar baseline.
Ti and Zr variations showed a nonmonotonic response: initial addition lowered tensile strength, while higher content produced a recovery.
Heating Nb10 to 1200 K reduced its UTS from about 3.7–3.8 GPa to 0.3 GPa and its elastic modulus from 137.7 GPa to 8.35 GPa.
